pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📐 **Strand 3 — Geometry And Measurement**
Shape, space, measurement, position and movement — the mathematics of the world around us.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B7.3.3)
- B7.3.3.1 — Perform a single transformation (i.e. reflection and translation) on a 2D shape using graph paper (including technology) and describe the properties of the image under the transformation (i.e. congruence, similarity, etc.).

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- identify shapes and designs in real life that have line (fold) symmetry
- plot points and shapes on a coordinate plane and identify lines such as x = 0, y = 0, y = x and y = −1
- reflect shapes in the x-axis, the y-axis and the lines y = x and y = −x and state the coordinate rules
- translate shapes by a given vector and describe the movement
- verify congruence and similarity of shapes

pages.title: Line symmetry in everyday life
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Determine shapes in real life that have reflectional (or fold) symmetries.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.3.1.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Line of symmetry** — A shape has **line (reflectional or fold) symmetry** if it can be folded along a line so that one half fits exactly on top of the other. The fold line is called the **line (axis) of symmetry**.
[[fig:m7-f62|Figure 12.1: Designs with lines of symmetry (dashed)]]
Many Ghanaian designs are symmetrical: Adinkra symbols printed on cloth, kente patterns, stools, drums and the national flag's star. Butterflies, leaves and the human face also show (approximate) line symmetry.
## ✏️ Example 12.1
In how many different ways can one more square be shaded in this shape so that the whole shape has a line of symmetry?
[[fig:m7-f63]]
**Solution**
Test each unshaded square:
Shading the **top-left** square gives a vertical line of symmetry (down the middle column).
Shading the **bottom-right** square gives a horizontal line of symmetry (along the middle row).
No other square works. So there are **2 ways**.
> 🧪 **Activity 12.1 — Adinkra symmetry**
Collect pictures of Adinkra symbols (e.g. Adinkrahene, Dwennimmen, Funtunfunefu, Akoma) or sketch them. Use a mirror or tracing paper to find all their lines of symmetry. Then design your own symmetrical symbol and give it a meaning.

pages.title: Exercise 12.1
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 12.1** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. How many lines of symmetry does each have? a) a square b) a rectangle c) an equilateral triangle d) a circle e) a regular hexagon f) the letter H g) the letter N
2. Which capital letters of the alphabet have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have a horizontal line of symmetry?
3. Copy a grid of 3 rows and 4 columns. Shade 4 squares so that the pattern has exactly 2 lines of symmetry.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does each have?
Which capital letters of the alphabet have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have a horizontal line of symmetry?

parts.a: Vertical: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y. Horizontal: B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X.

questions.q: Copy a grid of 3 rows and 4 columns. Shade 4 squares so that the pattern has exactly 2 lines of symmetry.

parts.a: e.g. shade the 4 squares of the middle row, or the 4 corner squares. (Each has one vertical and one horizontal line of symmetry.)

pages.title: Points, lines and shapes on the coordinate plane
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Plot points and shapes (plane figures) on a coordinate plane and draw their images under reflection in given lines.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.3.1.2
## ✏️ Example 12.2
Plot the points A(3, 1), B(3, 3), C(4, 3), D(4, 2), E(5, 2), F(5, 3), H(6, 3) and I(6, 1). Join them in order and join I to A. What shape do you get?
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f64]]
Figure 12.2: The points form a shape like the letter "m"
## ✏️ Example 12.3
Name the lines drawn on the number plane.
[[fig:m7-f65]]
Figure 12.3: Lines on the number plane
**Solution**
Line 1 is the **y-axis** (x = 0). Line 2 is the **x-axis** (y = 0). Line 3 is the line **y = x**. Line 4 is the line **y = −x**. Line 5 is the line **y = −1** (parallel to the x-axis). Line 6 is the line **x = 3** (parallel to the y-axis).
> 🔑 **Key idea: Lines parallel to the axes** — Every point on the line **x = a** has x-coordinate a; the line is vertical (parallel to the y-axis). Every point on the line **y = b** has y-coordinate b; the line is horizontal (parallel to the x-axis).
## Reflection
> 🔑 **Key idea: Reflection** — A **reflection** flips a shape over a **mirror line**. Each point of the image is the same perpendicular distance from the mirror line as the object point, but on the opposite side. The image is the same shape and size as the object (it is **congruent**), but it is "turned over" (laterally inverted).

pages.title: Example 12.4
pages.body:
## ✏️ Example 12.4
a) Draw A₁ as the image of A(1, 1) under a reflection in the y-axis (x = 0). b) Draw P as the image of A(1, 1) under a reflection in the x-axis (y = 0). c) Draw the image of P under a reflection in the line y = x.
**Solution**
a) A₁ = **(−1, 1)** b) P = **(1, −1)** c) P(1, −1) → **(−1, 1)**, which is the point A₁.
## ✏️ Example 12.5
Triangle ABC has vertices A(1, 1), B(4, 1) and C(4, 3). Draw its images under reflection in a) the x-axis b) the y-axis c) the line y = x. Compare the images.
**Solution**
[[fig:m7-f66]]
Figure 12.4: Triangle ABC and its images
a) In the x-axis: A′(1, −1), B′(4, −1), C′(4, −3)
b) In the y-axis: A″(−1, 1), B″(−4, 1), C″(−4, 3)
c) In y = x: A‴(1, 1), B‴(1, 4), C‴(3, 4)
All three images are **congruent** to ABC (same lengths and angles), but each faces the opposite way.
> 🔑 **Key idea: Coordinate rules for reflection** — Reflection in the **x-axis**: (a, b) → (a, −b). In the **y-axis**: (a, b) → (−a, b). In the line **y = x**: (a, b) → (b, a). In the line **y = −x**: (a, b) → (−b, −a).
> ✨ **Did you know?** A reflection can also be **in a point** (a half-turn about that point): reflecting (a, b) in the origin gives (−a, −b).

pages.title: Exercise 12.2
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 12.2** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. Plot the points P(2, 5), Q(−3, 4), R(−1, −2) and S(4, −3). State the quadrant each lies in.
2. Write down the equation of: a) the x-axis b) the line through (2, 5) and (2, −1) c) the line through (−3, 4) and (6, 4)
3. Find the image of (5, −2) under reflection in: a) the x-axis b) the y-axis c) y = x d) y = −x
4. Triangle PQR has P(2, 1), Q(5, 1), R(2, 4). Draw PQR and its image under reflection in the y-axis. Write the coordinates of the image.
5. The image of a point under reflection in the line y = x is (−4, 7). Find the point.
6. Reflect the square with vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (3, 3), (1, 3) in the line x = 4. Give the coordinates of the image.

pages.title: Translation
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Plot points and shapes on a coordinate plane and draw their images under translation by a given vector.
Curriculum indicator B7.3.3.1.3
> 🔑 **Key idea: Translation** — A **translation** slides every point of a shape the **same distance in the same direction**, without turning or flipping it. A translation is described by a **translation vector** col{a;b}: (x, y) → (x + a, y + b). The image is congruent to the object and faces the same way.
> 🌍 **Maths in real life** As children go down a slide, ride an escalator, or as a drawer is pulled out, they undergo a translation — every point moves the same distance in the same direction.
## ✏️ Example 12.6
Triangle PQR has vertices P(1, 1), Q(4, 1) and R(1, 3). Translate it by the vector col{3;2} and describe the change in the vertices.
**Solution**
Add 3 to each x-coordinate and 2 to each y-coordinate:
P(1, 1) → P′(4, 3); Q(4, 1) → Q′(7, 3); R(1, 3) → R′(4, 5)
[[fig:m7-f67]]
Figure 12.5: Translation of PQR by the vector (3, 2)
Every vertex moves 3 units to the right and 2 units up. Side lengths and angles are unchanged.
## ✏️ Example 12.7
Describe the single transformation that maps the shape PART onto P′A′R′T′ in the diagram.
[[fig:m7-f68]]
Figure 12.6: PART and its image P′A′R′T′
**Solution**
P(−4, 1) → P′(1, −2): the shape moves 5 right and 3 down without turning. It is a **translation by the vector** col{5;−3}.

3. Draw the square A(0, 0), B(2, 0), C(2, 2), D(0, 2) and its image under the translation col{−3;1}.
4. The point (5, 1) is mapped onto (2, 4) by a translation. Find the translation vector, and use it to find the image of (−1, −1).

pages.title: Congruent and similar shapes
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Verify the concept of congruent and similar shapes in the coordinate plane using properties of both object and image, and in real-life situations (carpet designs, fabric patterns).
Curriculum indicator B7.3.3.1.4
> 🔑 **Key idea: Congruent and similar** — Two shapes are **congruent** if they have exactly the same shape **and** size (all corresponding sides and angles are equal). Two shapes are **similar** if they have the same shape but may differ in size: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
Images under reflection and translation are always **congruent** to the object. Fabric prints, floor tiles and carpet designs often repeat congruent shapes; photographs and their enlargements are similar.
## ✏️ Example 12.8
Which shapes are congruent and which are similar?
[[fig:m7-f69]]
Figure 12.7: Compare the shapes
**Solution**
**A and D are congruent** (both are 2 × 3 rectangles; D is A turned).
**A and C are similar but not congruent**: C is 4 × 6, so every side is twice as long and the angles are all 90°.
**B and E are congruent** right-angled triangles (legs 3 and 2).
B and F are similar: F has legs 6 and 4, twice those of B.

pages.title: Exercise 12.4
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 12.4** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. Are all squares similar? Are all rectangles similar? Explain.
2. On graph paper draw triangle (0, 0), (3, 0), (0, 2). Draw a congruent triangle and a similar (but not congruent) triangle.
3. Look at a piece of printed cloth. Describe one pattern made from congruent shapes.

questions.q: Are all squares similar? Are all rectangles similar? Explain.

parts.a: All squares are similar (same angles, sides always in the same ratio). Not all rectangles are similar: a 2 × 3 rectangle and a 2 × 5 rectangle have different side ratios.

questions.q: On graph paper draw triangle (0, 0), (3, 0), (0, 2). Draw a congruent triangle and a similar (but not congruent) triangle.
Look at a piece of printed cloth. Describe one pattern made from congruent shapes.

pages.title: Chapter 12 summary
pages.body:
- A line of symmetry divides a shape into two mirror-image halves.
- x = a is a vertical line; y = b is a horizontal line.
- Reflection rules: x-axis (a, −b); y-axis (−a, b); y = x (b, a); y = −x (−b, −a).
- Translation by col{a;b}: (x, y) → (x + a, y + b).
- Reflections and translations give congruent images. Similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides.

questions.q: Draw a shape with exactly one line of symmetry and a shape with exactly three.

parts.a: e.g. an isosceles triangle; an equilateral triangle

questions.q: Find the image of (−3, 5) under reflection in:
Triangle ABC has A(1, 2), B(3, 2), C(1, 5). Reflect it in the x-axis and then translate the image by col{−4;0}. Give the final coordinates.
Which transformation maps (2, 7) onto (7, 2)? Give two possible answers.

parts.a: Reflection in y = x, or translation by col{5;−5}

questions.q: A rectangle measures 4 cm by 6 cm. Is a rectangle 6 cm by 9 cm similar to it? Explain.

parts.a: Yes: 6 ÷ 4 = 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5, so the sides are in the same ratio and all angles are 90°.
